title: How to heal from overcommitment
author: Kate Sotsenko
summary: Kate Sotsenko asks why busy professionals say yes when they clearly lack the time or energy to be present, and how to stop. Using the image of an overpacked hiking backpack, she names five drivers of overcommitment: the belief that doing more is how you achieve, an endless appetite for more fed by social media, the helper's addiction to the good feeling of being asked, the use of busyness as a way to avoid what is at the bottom of the bag, and a click-driven world that makes committing frictionless. Her remedy is not discipline or willpower but learning to say no to yourself, framed as kindness toward oneself. She links overcommitment directly to burnout and ends with a weekly challenge to say no to yourself at least once.
points: Overcommitment is like an overpacked backpack in which every yes adds weight and makes burnout more likely.
Five drivers sit behind it: the doing-more goal, the appetite for more, the helper's addiction, running away from what we avoid, and frictionless one-click commitments.
Sotsenko argues that so-called people pleasers are really self-pleasers who enjoy the reward of being asked for help.
Her fix is to say no to herself, as an act of kindness rather than discipline or willpower.
The weekly play is to say no to yourself at least once to lighten the backpack.
quotes: Overcommitment works the same way. Everything you say yes to goes inside your backpack
Every yes is a decision. To make more intentional decisions you have to understand what drives them.
But we need to be honest: we’re not people pleasers, we’re self-pleasers. And it’s just human.
It’s a form of subconscious procrastination. You add things in your backpack to cover those hidden at the very bottom.
It’s not discipline, it’s not will-power, it’s just kindness. Towards myself. Because the correlation between overcommitment and burnout is simple
Don’t aim to be disciplined. Just be kind to yourself first.
